365.title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45)
365.hook: he weeps so loudly all Egypt hears, and forgives
365.tomorrow: you thought evil, God turned it to good
365.howItsDone: In the sacrament of reconciliation, Catholics name their sins plainly and hear words of absolution, and many parishes point to stories like Joseph and his brothers when they preach on forgiving others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the brothers came for grain, and when Benjamin was caught with the silver cup, Judah offered to stay as a slave in his place. Your line was judah stepped forward. Whose load did you offer to carry? Day three hundred sixty-five.

Judah has just finished speaking. He's begged to be a slave so the boy can go home to their old father. The room is silent. And the governor of Egypt, the most powerful man in the country after Pharaoh, can't hold it anymore. He orders every Egyptian out of the room. Servants, guards, the interpreter, all of them. Then, alone with eleven frightened men from Canaan, he starts to cry. Not quietly. The text says he wept so loud that the Egyptians outside heard it, and word reached Pharaoh's house. Picture the brothers, standing there, waiting for a sentence, and hearing that instead.
screen: `JUDAH FINISHES. SILENCE.` → `EVERYONE OUT.` → `A CRY ALL EGYPT HEARS.`

segments.voice: Then two words in Hebrew, three in English: "I am Joseph." And straight after, before anything else, a question: is my father still alive? The brothers can't answer. The text says they were terrified at his presence. Of course they were. The boy they sold is now the man who decides whether they eat or starve. So Joseph says, come close. And they come, and he says it again, more fully this time: I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt. He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. He names it, out loud, in front of all of them. Then he says something no one in that room expected: don't be grieved, don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to keep you alive. It wasn't you who sent me here, he says, but God. He doesn't erase what they did. He sets it inside something larger. Then he falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps, and kisses all his brothers, one by one. And here is the line that's easy to miss: after that, his brothers talked with him. Twenty years of silence, and now they're just talking. Last, a small human detail as he loads their donkeys with Egyptian gifts and sends them home to bring Jacob: don't quarrel on the way. A family that sold a brother, and the brother's last advice is, please don't fight in the car. When the news reaches Jacob, his heart goes numb, he doesn't believe it. Then he sees the wagons Joseph sent, and he says: Joseph my son is still alive; I'll go and see him before I die.
screen: `EVERYONE OUT. THEN THE TEARS.` · `I AM JOSEPH. IS MY FATHER ALIVE?` · `NOT YOU, BUT GOD, SENT ME HERE.` · `DON'T QUARREL ON THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one old grudge go. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come to mind, someone who hurt you, maybe long ago, maybe in a way you still replay. Notice that Joseph didn't pretend. He said what they did, plainly. You can do that too: name what happened, silently, without softening it. Then see if you can loosen your grip on it, even a little. Letting go isn't the same as saying it was fine. If you pray, you can hand the grudge to God for these two minutes. If you don't, just notice what your hands feel like when they open. The bell holds the time.
I am Joseph. The words the governor of Egypt says to the brothers who sold him, through tears, before he forgives them. Today's word.
Your line: I am your brother. Today, if an old grudge comes back, name it honestly once, then set it down instead of rehearsing it. Day three hundred sixty-five.

366.title: You thought evil, God turned it to good (Genesis 50:15–21)
366.hook: Joseph's last word to his brothers on their fear
366.howItsDone: The Catechism of the Catholic Church teaches divine providence in its opening section on creation (paragraphs 302–314), and uses Joseph's words to his brothers as an example of God drawing good out of evil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am Joseph: a cry all Egypt heard, and a brother who named the wrong and forgave it. Your line was I am your brother. Did an old grudge loosen? Today, the last day of Genesis. Day three hundred sixty-six.

Seventeen years later, Jacob dies in Egypt. They carry him home to Canaan and bury him with Abraham and Isaac. And the moment the funeral is over, the brothers panic. Their father was the reason Joseph was kind to them, they think. Now he's gone. What if Joseph was only waiting? So they send a message: before he died, our father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. Then they come themselves, fall down in front of him, and say: we are your servants. Whether Jacob ever really said that, the text doesn't tell us. It only tells us what Joseph does when he hears it. He weeps.
screen: `JACOB DIES.` → `THE BROTHERS PANIC.` → `WE ARE YOUR SERVANTS.`

segments.voice: Then his answer, the last thing Joseph says to his brothers in the Bible's first book. Don't be afraid, he tells them. And then: "You thought evil against me: but God turned it into good," to save many people alive. He doesn't say it wasn't evil. It was. He doesn't say God made them do it. He says two things happened at once: their plan, and God's. Today's word for that is providence. It comes from Latin, providere, to see ahead and so to provide. The Church's Catechism says God guides all of creation toward its goal, and that God is never the author of evil, yet can draw good even out of it. And when it reaches for an example, it uses this very story: Joseph telling his brothers it wasn't they who sent him, but God. Then the Catechism goes further, to the cross. The worst thing human beings ever did, it says, God turned into the greatest good. That's how Catholics hear this verse: as a first sketch of Good Friday and Easter. Now look back at the whole of Genesis, these thirty-odd days. It opened with in the beginning: light, then six days and a rest. Dust and breath. A serpent, and a question, where art thou. A brother who asked if he was his brother's keeper. Noah building, a bow in the clouds, Babel. Abraham told to go forth, counting stars, and on a mountain saying God will provide. And it ends here, with a brother answering that old question about keepers. Genesis begins with a garden and ends with a coffin in Egypt, and a promise that God will come for his people.
screen: `YOU THOUGHT EVIL AGAINST ME.` · `GOD TURNED IT INTO GOOD.` · `PROVIDENCE: TO SEE AHEAD, AND PROVIDE.` · `FROM A GARDEN TO A COFFIN IN EGYPT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for good that grew from a wound. Settle, and breathe. Think of something that hurt, a loss, a betrayal, a door that closed. Don't pretend it was good. It wasn't. Just look, gently, at what grew around it afterward. A friend you wouldn't have met. Something you understand now that you didn't. A kindness you can offer because you know that pain. If nothing has grown yet, that's honest too. If you pray, you can thank God for one good thing without calling the wound good. If you don't, simply notice both, side by side. The bell holds the time.
Providence. God's seeing ahead and guiding all things, never causing evil, yet able to draw good out of it. Today's word.
Your line: god turned it to good. Today, tell someone about one good thing that came out of a hard time, and don't skip the hard part. Day three hundred sixty-six.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything happens for a reason, so it was fine.

what a scholar hears: in Hebrew Joseph asks am I in the place of God?; the Latin Vulgate, and so the Douay-Rheims, renders 50:19 as a question about resisting God's will.

367.title: The midwives (Exodus 1)
367.hook: Shiphrah and Puah refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the boys
367.howItsDone: Catholic teaching on conscience holds that a person must refuse a command from any authority that would require a grave wrong, and Catholic writers on the defense of life often point to Shiphrah and Puah as early examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, providence: Joseph told his frightened brothers, you thought evil, but God turned it to good, and Genesis closed. What good did you find growing from a wound? Today a new book opens: Exodus. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

Exodus opens with a list of names, Jacob's sons who came down to Egypt, and then the family grows until the land is full of them. And then one quiet, chilling line: a new king arose over Egypt who knew not Joseph. All the grain, all the lives saved, forgotten in a generation. The new king looks at this growing people and sees a threat. So he puts them to forced labor, building store cities, making bricks, working the fields. And they keep growing. So he tries something worse. He calls in two women who deliver babies, and gives them an order. Today: the first two people in Exodus to say no to Pharaoh.
screen: `A KING WHO KNEW NOT JOSEPH.` → `BRICKS AND FORCED LABOR.` → `AN ORDER FOR TWO MIDWIVES.`

segments.voice: First, the order. When you help the Hebrew women give birth, Pharaoh says, if it's a boy, kill him; if it's a girl, let her live. Second, the refusal. The text says it simply: "But the midwives feared God." They didn't do what the king said. They let the boys live. Fear here isn't panic. It's the old biblical sense of reverence: they stood in awe of God more than of the most powerful man they'd ever meet. Third, the excuse. Pharaoh calls them back: why have you done this? And they answer, with a straight face, that Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women; they're vigorous, and they give birth before the midwife even gets there. It's a clever answer, maybe a sly one, and it keeps them alive. Fourth, the names. Notice who gets named in this chapter. The midwives do: Shiphrah and Puah. The Douay-Rheims spells them Sephora and Phua. The king of Egypt, the most powerful man on earth, never gets a name at all. The text says God dealt well with the midwives and gave them households of their own. Nobody knows for sure whether they were Hebrew women or Egyptian women who served the Hebrews; the Hebrew can be read either way. The Church has long honored this kind of courage. Its Catechism says a citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow orders of civil authorities that go against the moral order. Peter put it in one line in Acts: "We ought to obey God, rather than men." Two women in a birthing room said it first. The chapter ends darkly: Pharaoh orders every newborn boy thrown into the Nile. Tomorrow, one of them is put in a basket.
screen: `IF IT'S A BOY, KILL HIM.` · `BUT THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD.` · `THEY'RE QUICK; WE COME TOO LATE.` · `THE MIDWIVES ARE NAMED. PHARAOH ISN'T.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one small wrong you can refuse. Settle, and breathe. Most of us will never face a Pharaoh. But small orders come all day: pass along the rumor, fudge the number, laugh at the joke about the person who isn't there, look away. Think of one you're likely to meet this week. Picture it clearly. Then picture yourself quietly not doing it. No speech, no drama, just a no. If you pray, you can ask for the midwives' kind of courage. If you don't, just rehearse that no until it feels like your own. The bell holds the time.
The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who feared God more than Pharaoh, and let the Hebrew boys live. Today's word.
Your line: two women said no. Today, when a small wrong is handed to you, set it down instead of passing it on. Day three hundred sixty-seven.

368.title: The basket in the reeds (Exodus 2:1–10)
368.hook: a mother, a sister watching, and Pharaoh's daughter who pities the child
368.howItsDone: Catholic art and preaching have long linked the infant Moses, saved from a king's order to kill the boys, with the infant Jesus, carried to safety in Egypt when Herod ordered the killing of the children of Bethlehem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the midwives: Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh and let the boys live. Your line was two women said no. What small wrong did you refuse? Day three hundred sixty-eight.

Pharaoh's order is out: every Hebrew baby boy goes into the Nile. And in one house of the tribe of Levi, a boy is born. His mother looks at him and sees, the text says, that he's a goodly child. So she hides him. One month. Two. Three. Anyone who's lived with a newborn knows how impossible that is: the crying at three in the morning, the neighbors, the walls. When she can't hide him any longer, she does something that sounds like obeying the order and is the opposite. She puts her son in the Nile. Just not the way Pharaoh meant.
screen: `EVERY BOY INTO THE NILE.` → `THREE MONTHS OF HIDING.` → `INTO THE NILE, HER WAY.`

segments.voice: First, the basket. She takes a basket of papyrus reeds, seals it with tar and pitch, lays the baby inside, and sets it among the reeds at the river's edge. The Hebrew word for this basket is tevah. It appears in only one other story in the Bible: Noah's ark. A boat that carries life through deadly water, again, only this time it's the size of a baby. Second, the sister. She stands at a distance, the text says, to see what will happen. She isn't named here. Later the Bible names Moses's sister as Miriam, and tradition has long taken her to be this girl. She just watches. Third, Pharaoh's daughter. She comes down to bathe, sees the basket, sends her maid to fetch it, and opens it. The baby is crying. And she has compassion on him, and says, this is one of the Hebrews' children. She knows exactly what he is, and whose order he's under. Her father's. And she pities him anyway. Fourth, the sister's move. She steps out of hiding, quick as anything: shall I go and find you a nurse from the Hebrew women? Go, says the princess. And the girl fetches the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter even pays her to nurse her own son. When he's older, the princess adopts him and names him Moses, because, she says, she drew him out of the water. So count the women before Moses says a single word: two midwives, a mother, a sister, a princess. The king's plan was to drown the boys. Every one of those women undid it.
screen: `A TEVAH: THE SAME WORD AS NOAH'S ARK.` · `A SISTER STANDS AT A DISTANCE.` · `THIS IS ONE OF THE HEBREWS' CHILDREN.` · `DRAWN OUT OF THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch over someone small. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who can't fully protect themselves: a child, a new neighbor who doesn't speak the language yet, an elderly relative, a kid at school who sits alone. You don't have to rescue anyone today. The sister in the reeds didn't. She just stayed close enough to see, and spoke up at the right moment. Picture that person, and ask where you could stand at a distance and keep watch. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. If you don't, just keep them in view for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The basket in the reeds. A mother's sealed papyrus basket on the Nile, a sister watching, and a princess who pities the child. Today's word.
screen: `THE BASKET IN THE REEDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a sister watched. Today, keep an eye out for someone small or overlooked, and be ready to speak up when the moment comes. Day three hundred sixty-eight.

369.title: The bush that burned (Exodus 3:1–6)
369.hook: put off the shoes from thy feet, for the place is holy ground
369.howItsDone: On Good Friday, the Roman Missal allows the priest to remove his chasuble and shoes before venerating the cross, and in Eastern Catholic churches the burning bush appears in icons of Mary, the Mother of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the basket in the reeds: a mother, a princess, and a sister who stood at a distance. Your line was a sister watched. Who did you keep in view? Day three hundred sixty-nine.

The baby from the basket grew up in Pharaoh's palace. Then one day, as a grown man, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, killed the Egyptian, and ran for his life. Now he's in the land of Midian, far from Egypt, married, keeping his father-in-law's sheep. The book of Acts says forty years go by. A prince who became a fugitive who became a shepherd. One day he leads the flock to the far side of the wilderness, to a mountain called Horeb. And out of the corner of his eye, he sees a bush on fire. That's not strange in a desert. What's strange is that it keeps burning, and doesn't burn up.
screen: `A PRINCE, A FUGITIVE, A SHEPHERD.` → `FORTY YEARS IN MIDIAN.` → `A BUSH THAT DOESN'T BURN UP.`

segments.voice: First, Moses turns aside. He says to himself, I'll go over and see this great sight, why the bush isn't burnt. That small detour is the hinge of his life. The text says when the Lord saw that he turned aside to look, God called to him out of the bush: Moses, Moses. And he answers, here I am. Second, the command. Not a speech, not a mission yet. Just this: "Come not nigh hither, put off the shoes from thy feet: for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." It's the same dirt Moses walked across a minute ago with his sheep. Nothing about the ground changed. What changed is who was there. Third, the face. God says, I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob. And Moses hides his face, afraid to look at God. Fourth, what Catholics see in the bush. Very early, Christian writers read this fire that burns without consuming as a picture of Mary: God dwelling within her, and her virginity kept whole. An old antiphon for the first of January, the feast of Mary, Mother of God, sings it: in the bush Moses saw unburnt, the Church recognizes her virginity preserved. The Hebrew word for bush, seneh, sounds a lot like Sinai, the mountain where this story will lead. And the shoes stay in Catholic practice too. On Good Friday, the Roman Missal allows the priest to take off his shoes before he comes forward to venerate the cross.
screen: `MOSES TURNS ASIDE TO SEE.` · `PUT OFF THE SHOES FROM THY FEET.` · `HE HIDES HIS FACE.` · `THE BUSH UNBURNT: A PICTURE OF MARY.` · then, large: `HOLY GROUND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take off your shoes and stand still. If you can, do it literally. Slip them off. Feel the floor under your bare feet, its temperature, its texture. If you can't, just press your feet into the ground where you are. Now stand, or sit, and do nothing. The place hasn't changed. It's your kitchen, your bedroom, your office. Let it be the ground Moses stood on for two minutes. If you pray, you can simply say, here I am. If you don't, let the stillness be enough, and notice what it's like to treat an ordinary floor with reverence. The bell holds the time.
The bush that burned. A desert bush on fire and not consumed, where God called Moses by name and the ground became holy. Today's word.
Your line: holy ground. Today, pick one ordinary place, a doorway, a sink, a bus stop, and treat it once as if it were holy ground. Day three hundred sixty-nine.

370.title: Who am I (Exodus 3:11–4:17)
370.hook: Moses gives five excuses, including I'm slow of speech
370.howItsDone: Catholics pray the angel's greeting to Mary, "the Lord is with thee," in every Hail Mary, and the Church often reads call stories like Moses's on vocation Sundays, when parishes pray for priests, religious and lay ministers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bush that burned and wasn't consumed, and a voice saying take off your shoes. Your line was holy ground. Where did you stand still today? Day three hundred seventy.

You've been asked to do something too big for you. Give the toast. Lead the project. Have the hard conversation with your father. And your mind starts producing reasons, very reasonable ones, why it should really be someone else. Moses is standing barefoot in front of a burning bush, and God has just told him the plan: I've seen my people's misery in Egypt, I've heard their cry, and I'm sending you to Pharaoh to bring them out. And Moses, the man who'll become the greatest prophet of Israel, does exactly what we do. He starts making excuses. Five of them.
screen: `TOO BIG FOR YOU.` → `I'M SENDING YOU TO PHARAOH.` → `FIVE EXCUSES.`

segments.voice: Excuse one: who am I, to go to Pharaoh? A fair question from a shepherd with a past. And God doesn't answer it. God doesn't say, you're actually very talented. God says, "I will be with thee." The answer to who am I is who goes with you. Excuse two: what if they ask your name? God gives the name, I am who am, which this path opened back in year one. Excuse three: they won't believe me. So God gives signs: the staff that becomes a snake, the hand that turns white and heals, water from the Nile that turns to blood. Excuse four is the most human: I'm not a speaker. I never have been, not before and not since you started talking to me; I'm slow of speech and slow of tongue. Jewish tradition and many readers since have wondered whether Moses had a stammer; the text doesn't say. God's reply is almost funny: who made a person's mouth? Go, and I'll be with your mouth. And then excuse five, with nothing left: please, Lord, send someone else. That's the one that makes God angry. And still God doesn't fire him. God sends his brother Aaron along to help him speak. Catholics hear an echo of this scene in a small house in Nazareth. An angel greets a young woman with the words, "the Lord is with thee," and gives her an impossible mission. She asks one honest question, how shall this be done, gets her answer, and says yes. Moses took five tries. The promise was the same both times: you won't go alone.
screen: `WHO AM I? I WILL BE WITH THEE.` · `THEY WON'T BELIEVE ME: SIGNS.` · `I'M SLOW OF SPEECH: WHO MADE YOUR MOUTH?` · `SEND SOMEONE ELSE: AARON GOES TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your excuse, then go anyway. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you've been avoiding because it feels too big: a call, an apology, a class, a conversation. Now listen to the reason you give yourself. Say it plainly, the way Moses did. I'm not good with words. I'm not the right person. They won't listen. Don't argue with it. Just name it. Then picture yourself doing the thing anyway, excuse and all, with someone beside you. If you pray, you can hear God's answer to Moses: I will be with thee. If you don't, picture a friend at your shoulder. The bell holds the time.
Who am I. Moses's first excuse at the burning bush, answered not with praise but with a promise of presence. Today's word.
Your line: I will be with thee. Today, take one small step toward the thing you've been excusing yourself from. Day three hundred seventy.

371.title: Let my people go (Exodus 5–10)
371.hook: bricks without straw, then plagues against a hardened heart
371.howItsDone: Catholic social teaching, beginning with Pope Leo XIII's letter Rerum Novarum in 1891, defends workers' right to a just wage, and the Catechism lists defrauding laborers of their wages among the sins that cry to heaven.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who am I: five excuses at the burning bush, and one answer under all of them. Your line was I will be with thee. Did you take the step? Today closes a week that ran from Joseph's tears through the midwives, the basket and the bush. Day three hundred seventy-one.

Moses and Aaron walk into Pharaoh's court and say four words that people have been singing ever since. "Let my people go." Enslaved people in America sang them in the spiritual Go Down, Moses. And Pharaoh's answer is a shrug: who is this Lord, that I should listen to him? I don't know him. Then he does something every bad boss in history would recognize. He doesn't argue. He raises the quota. Same number of bricks every day, he orders, but you won't be given straw anymore. Go find your own.
screen: `LET MY PEOPLE GO.` → `WHO IS THIS LORD?` → `SAME BRICKS, NO STRAW.`

segments.voice: First, the bricks. The Hebrews scatter across Egypt gathering stubble, and of course they can't make the count. So the Egyptian taskmasters beat the Hebrew foremen. The foremen go to Pharaoh and get nowhere, and on the way out they turn on Moses: you've made us stink in Pharaoh's eyes. And Moses turns to God: why did you ever send me? Things got worse the moment I spoke. Second, the plagues. Blood in the Nile. Frogs everywhere. Gnats. Flies. Sickness on the cattle. Boils. Hail. Locusts. Then darkness so thick it can be felt. Nine in these chapters; the tenth comes tomorrow. Pharaoh's magicians copy the first ones, then give up at the gnats and tell him: this is the finger of God. Third, the hard heart. Over and over Pharaoh promises to let the people go, then changes his mind when the trouble lifts. Sometimes the text says Pharaoh hardened his own heart. Later it says God hardened it. Readers have wrestled with that for centuries. Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas Aquinas taught that God doesn't put evil into anyone; when God is said to harden a heart, it means God withholds grace from someone who has already chosen to refuse it. Fourth, the cry. This is a story about bricks and wages and bodies, not only souls. The Catholic Church has long said that cheating workers of a just wage is a sin that cries out to heaven, and in 1891 Pope Leo the Thirteenth wrote a whole letter on the rights of workers. That teaching leans on stories like this one: God hearing the cry of people forced to work without straw.
screen: `BRICKS WITHOUT STRAW.` · `NINE PLAGUES, AND THE FINGER OF GOD.` · `A HEART THAT KEEPS HARDENING.` · `A CRY THAT REACHES HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember workers treated unjustly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work you depend on and rarely see: whoever picked the fruit in your kitchen, sewed the shirt you're wearing, cleans the building you work in, drives the truck that brought your packages. Some of them are paid fairly. Some are making bricks without straw. Let one face come to mind, even an imagined one. If you pray, you can pray for them by name or by work, using Moses's words: let my people go. If you don't, just hold them in mind with respect for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Let my people go. God's demand to Pharaoh through Moses, answered with heavier work and a heart that kept hardening. Today's word.
Your line: let my people go. Today, look up who makes one thing you use every day, and thank one worker you'd usually walk past. Day three hundred seventy-one.
